contexts.text:
A smaller exhibition stand

Fictional practice account. A design team built two models of an exhibition stand. The first used a heavy wooden frame and was difficult to move. The second used fewer panels and a lighter frame while retaining enough support for the planned display. The team kept a log of changes and tested the models in the classroom. The report described this as an improvement for their own project. It did not claim that the design was suitable for constructing a full-size public building.

A device for shared notices

Fictional practice instructions. The club’s notice screen displays a local timetable. Members can scroll through the pages using two large buttons. An editor updates the information from a nearby computer; ordinary visitors can read it but cannot change it. The device stores a copy of the last timetable so it can still display that version if the connection fails. A small label shows the date of the most recent update. The design aims to be user-friendly, rather than offer as many features as possible.

A cooperative market stall

Fictional practice account. Two small producers formed a joint venture to share a weekend stall. One made wooden toys and the other printed greeting cards. Each kept its own business, but they divided the cost of the stall and took turns serving customers. Their products attracted different visitors, giving both a chance to reach a wider market. Their short report called the arrangement useful so far, while recognising that a few successful weekends did not guarantee future earnings.

A compromise over a meeting room

Fictional practice account. A residents’ group wanted to use a community room every evening, while a youth club needed the same space twice a week. Both groups initially presented the issue as a competition. At a joint meeting they identified which activities really needed the larger room. The residents accepted two smaller-room sessions, and the youth club agreed to finish early on one evening. The compromise addressed the immediate difficulty without assuming that either group’s needs were unimportant.

An energy trial with limits

Fictional practice account. A learning centre compared its electricity readings during two fictional trial periods. In the second period it used a more efficient lighting arrangement and changed its opening hours. Recorded consumption was lower. The report did not assign the whole reduction to the lights because two conditions had changed together. It proposed a further trial with the same opening hours. The example teaches the difference between a measured result and a confident explanation of its cause.

An imagined part-time position

Fictional practice advertisement. A community workshop seeks a part-time reception assistant for two afternoons each week. Duties include greeting visitors, keeping a booking record and answering enquiries. Experience with a simple spreadsheet is useful, and training is provided. Applicants should send a short covering letter and CV, explaining their relevant experience and availability. The advert does not state the pay. It asks applicants to enquire about any details they need before accepting a position.

A headline and the evidence

Fictional practice passage. A local club held a trial repair event attended by thirty visitors. Its report stated that twenty-two people completed feedback forms. One online headline described the event as a success for the whole town. The report itself contained no town-wide survey. A reader could reasonably say that the event took place and that forms were collected. Judging the whole town’s opinion would require more evidence. The passage does not say what proportion of visitors were already club members.

Different responses to one exhibition

Fictional practice account. Two friends visited an exhibition of paintings and wooden carvings. One preferred vivid abstract pictures, while the other liked detailed portraits. Both admired the craftsmanship of the carvings. They wrote separate reviews and used examples to explain their tastes. The gallery quoted each judgement with the writer’s name, rather than describing either preference as a measurement of universal artistic quality. Their disagreement made the discussion more interesting without requiring one person’s taste to be declared wrong.

An original dictionary entry

Original practice entry. Record, noun: a written or stored account kept so that information can be checked later. Plural: records. Example: The organiser kept a record of each booking. Record, verb: put information into a written or stored form. Example: We record the results after each trial. These independently written entries illustrate why a learner should check grammatical role and context. A single spelling does not guarantee that every occurrence has the same form, pronunciation or use.

A clear short argument

Original writing-practice model. I believe students benefit from continuing to develop writing skills after primary school. Early lessons introduce letters and basic sentences. Later tasks require students to compare evidence, explain unfamiliar ideas and adapt their language to different readers. For example, a friendly invitation and a formal application need different tones. This does not make early learning unimportant; rather, it gives students a foundation on which to build. Therefore, continued guidance can help learners use writing more flexibly.

A formal enquiry

Original fictional letter model. Dear Ms Rahimi, I am writing to enquire about the weekend design course advertised by your centre. I have some experience making classroom displays and would like to develop my practical skills. Could you confirm whether beginners can attend and whether materials are included? I would also be grateful for information about the timetable and any work expected between sessions. Thank you in advance for your help. I look forward to hearing from you. Yours sincerely, Neda Farah.
